resources.string: Gentians often have opposite leaves and regular flowers with a fused corolla; fruits commonly form capsules.
Tropical trees and shrubs, often with strongly veined toothed leaves and numerous stamens; persistent sepals may enlarge around fruitlets.
A diverse family with varied flowers; Euphorbia species have a specialized cyathium and often milky latex.
Often recognizable by swollen stem nodes and small flowers; fruits commonly are three-angled achenes.
Aquatic rhizomatous herbs with floating or emergent leaves and solitary flowers above or at the water surface.

A solitary blue-green cactus ranging from flattened-globose to short-columnar. Its 5–8 ribs bear areoles marked by conspicuous white woolly scales and stout spines; pale yellow flowers arise at the crown.
Native to north-eastern Mexico, from Coahuila and San Luis Potosí toward Veracruz; inhabits dry scrub and rocky slopes.
Single ribbed cactus with white areoles and spines
An evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and narrow crown. Flattened sprays carry opposite scale-like leaves; its small seed cones have four principal scales, while pollen cones occur in clusters.
Native from southern China and Hainan through northern Indochina, including Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam.

A small annual or biennial gentian, usually with a basal rosette and upright, often branched stems. Opposite leaves accompany terminal clusters of pink, five-lobed flowers; the fruit is a narrow capsule with many minute seeds.
Native across much of Europe, North Africa and western Asia; now introduced in many temperate regions.

A tree-like columnar cactus of seasonally dry Brazil, with erect branching stems and several prominent ribs bearing areoles and spines. Large white flowers open at night; oblong red fruits contain white pulp and dark seeds.
Native to central and eastern Brazil, especially the Caatinga and other seasonally dry landscapes.

A low tuberous perennial whose rounded, kidney-shaped leaves often show silvery patterns. Short-stalked flowers have five rounded petals reflexed upward, commonly pink with a darker basal mark; the fruiting stalk coils toward the ground.
Native from south-eastern Europe across the Caucasus and western Asia to Israel; flowers in the cool season.
Tuber, patterned leaves and reflexed flowers

A large evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and broad conical crown. Stiff, sharply pointed linear leaves spiral around the shoots; rounded to broadly ovoid female cones bear broad overlapping scales, and pollen cones form clusters.
Native to central and southern China, extending into northern Vietnam; widely cultivated elsewhere.

An evergreen tropical tree with large alternate, strongly veined leaves and toothed margins. Solitary white flowers have numerous petals and stamens; after flowering, enlarged persistent sepals become fleshy around the clustered fruitlets.
Native to the Indian subcontinent and mainland South-East Asia; cultivated in tropical gardens and for its fruit.

An erect tropical evergreen herb with stout, ring-scarred cane-like stems and large alternate leaves. The inflorescence is a cream spadix partly enclosed by a green spathe; berries ripen orange-red. Sap and tissues contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are poisonous.
Native to the Caribbean and tropical America; widely cultivated as a houseplant.

An endemic evergreen tree with a stout trunk and a distinctive umbrella-shaped crown of repeatedly forked branches. Stiff linear leaves cluster at branch tips; branched inflorescences bear pale flowers followed by fleshy orange-red berries.
Endemic to Socotra, Yemen, where it grows on rocky plateaux and mountain slopes; the 2004 IUCN assessment listed it as Vulnerable.

A slender, clumping palm with several ringed stems and arching pinnate leaves. Branched inflorescences emerge below the crown and carry small flowers; ripe fruits are round, dark purple drupes with a large seed and a thin edible pulp, commonly processed as food.
Native to the Amazon basin of northern South America, especially seasonally flooded forests and estuaries.

A rhizomatous perennial that forms dense upright patches of slender stems. Numerous narrow linear leaves give it a cypress-like outline; the terminal yellow-green structures are cyathia, each a tiny flower cluster enclosed by an involucre. The milky latex can irritate skin and eyes.
Native to Europe and western Asia; introduced and locally invasive in parts of North America.

A small annual with hairy reddish stems, usually prostrate or ascending. Opposite oblong leaves may have a dark central blotch; compact cyathia occur in axillary clusters, followed by small three-lobed capsules. Its latex is irritating; traditional names do not establish medicinal safety.
Native to tropical and subtropical America; now pantropical and widespread in warm regions.

A robust coastal perennial with a deep rootstock and stiff, glaucous, spiny leaves. Its branched stems bear rounded heads of tiny blue flowers surrounded by rigid spiny bracts; the dry fruit splits into two mericarps.
Native to Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts of Europe and North Africa, extending east into western Asia; characteristic of coastal dunes.

A small, blue-green, flattened-globose cactus with distinct ribs and widely spaced areoles. Curved stout spines give the plant its common name; pink to magenta flowers appear at the crown and are followed by small reddish fruits with woolly scales.
Native to arid regions of the south-western United States and northern Mexico, on limestone and rocky slopes.

A fast-growing, upright columnar cactus with several blue-green stems, usually 6–8 broad ribs and small areoles with short spines. Large white flowers open at night, and green ovoid fruits develop later. “San Pedro” is a common name also applied to related cacti, so it is not by itself a reliable identification.
Native to the Andean region of Ecuador and Peru; cultivated widely beyond its native range.

An annual crop with reddish branching stems, alternate triangular leaves and loose clusters of small white or pink flowers. Its dry fruit is a distinctive three-angled achene enclosing one seed; the crop is used as a food grain despite not being a true cereal grass.
Cultivated worldwide; domesticated in temperate East Asia and the Himalayan region.

A large deciduous North American tree with smooth pale grey bark and a spreading crown. Alternate oval leaves have straight side veins ending at the teeth; male catkins hang from twigs, while prickly four-valved husks enclose two sharply three-angled nuts.
Native to eastern North America, from southern Canada through the eastern United States.
Oval leaf with straight parallel veins

A perennial with slender erect stems and narrow leaves arranged in conspicuous whorls. Dense airy panicles carry numerous tiny yellow four-lobed flowers; the fruit separates into two smooth rounded nutlets.
Native across Europe and temperate Asia; found in dry grasslands, dunes and open scrub.

A boreal evergreen tree with a straight trunk and symmetrical conical crown. Stiff, four-angled needles attach singly around the twig and show pale stomatal lines; slender pendant seed cones have thin, rounded scales.
Native across Canada and Alaska, reaching the northern United States; characteristic of boreal and montane forests.

An aquatic perennial rooted by a thick, branching rhizome. Its floating oval leaves have a deep basal sinus where the petiole attaches; solitary yellow flowers form a cup of petaloid sepals, and the later fruit is a green, bottle-shaped capsule.
Native across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia to Siberia and Xinjiang, chiefly in still or slow-moving fresh water.
Rhizome, floating leaves and yellow cups
Leaf with basal sinus and petiole
